reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Syndactyly is failure of separation of adjacent digits and is the commonest congenital hand difference; it is classified as simple (soft tissue only) or complex (with bony fusion), and as complete (to the fingertips) or incomplete
Complicated syndactyly involves additional or abnormal bones, tendons, or neurovascular structures beyond a simple bony bridge
The third web space (long-ring) is most often affected; the condition is frequently bilateral and may be familial (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance)

Border-digit and unequal-length pairings (such as ring-little or thumb-index) should be separated earlier, because tethering causes progressive angular and rotational deformity as the digits grow at different rates

Syndromic links include Apert syndrome (complex symmetrical syndactyly producing a 'mitten hand'), Poland syndrome (with chest-wall and pectoral deficiency), and constriction ring (amniotic band) sequence
Surgical separation uses interdigitating (zig-zag) incisions to resurface the sides of the digits and reconstructs the web (commissure) with local flaps, frequently supplemented by skin grafts
The two sides of a single digit are generally not released at the same operation, so as to protect that digit's blood supply
reference.pathophysiology: Syndactyly results from failure of the normal programmed cell death (apoptosis) that separates the digital rays during limb development, so adjacent digits remain joined by skin and, in complex forms, by bone. It represents a failure of differentiation and may occur in isolation, be inherited, or form part of a syndrome in which broader signalling defects affect both the hand and other structures, as in the acrocephalosyndactyly of Apert syndrome or the vascular disruption of constriction ring sequence.
additionalDifferentials: Constriction ring (amniotic band) sequence with acrosyndactyly
Camptodactyly or clinodactyly (angular deformity without fusion)
Acquired web contracture from burn or trauma
Cleft hand with abnormal web spaces
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs to distinguish simple from complex (bony) syndactyly and to define shared skeletal structures
Careful clinical assessment of the affected web pairing and relative digit lengths
Screening for syndromic features (craniofacial in Apert, chest wall in Poland)
Vascular assessment and staged planning for complex or complete syndactyly
Genetic evaluation where the pattern is syndromic or strongly familial
redFlags: Complex or complicated syndactyly with a shared neurovascular bundle risking devascularisation at separation
Progressive deformity of border digits from tethered unequal growth
Features of Apert or another syndrome requiring multidisciplinary care
reference.prognosis: Simple isolated syndactyly has excellent results after zig-zag separation and web reconstruction; complex and syndromic forms, especially Apert syndrome, are more likely to need multiple procedures and to leave residual stiffness, distal migration of the web ('web creep'), and imperfect appearance.
pitfalls: Releasing both sides of the same digit at one operation and compromising its blood supply
Delaying separation of unequal-length border digits, allowing fixed deformity to develop
Reconstructing the web too shallow or narrow, leading to web creep
Underestimating shared bony or neurovascular anatomy in complex syndactyly
